newsitem.title: INDIA: India RBI, government agree on 1997/98 advances.
newsitem.headline: India RBI, government agree on 1997/98 advances.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the federal government on Wednesday signed an agreement to give effect to a new system of central bank funding to meet the government's borrowing needs in 1997/98 (April-March).

"The limit for ways and means advances will be 120 billion rupees ($3.35 billion) for the first half of the year (April-September) and 80 billion rupees ($2.23 billion) for the second half of the year (October-March)," RBI said in a statement.

RBI governor Chakravarti Rangarajan, who signed the agreement with Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia, told reporters that the advance limits referred to the limit at any point in time in the fiscal year.
It would be appropriate to see the overall limit in the year as the average of the two halves, he said.
The ways and means advances (WMA), which would take effect from April 1, will replace the existing system of ad-hoc treasury bills used by the government to raise funds.
The WMA would be used to bridge temporary mismatches between government receipts and payments.

Up to the ways and means limit, the government would pay interest at 3.0 percentage points below the average yield rates on the cut-off prices at 91-day treasury bill auctions held in the previous quarter, the RBI statement said.
For overdrafts beyond this limit, the interest rate would be 2.0 percentage points above the interest charged within the limit, the statement.
The decision to conclude the agreement signed on Wednesday was announced by Finance Minister P.Chidambaram in his speech while presenting the budget for 1997/98 on February 28.
Rangarajan said the new system would go through a transition period for two years before stabilising.

"WMA is not a source of financing and as such will not be shown as a source of financing the budget deficit. It is only a mechanism to cover day-to-day mismatches in receipts and payments of the government," the RBI statement said.
"Secondly, limits on WMA will be fixed any excess drawal byond the limit will not be permissible for more than ten consecutive days after March 1999," it added.
Besides, the WMA will be charged at market related interest rates, the statement said.

Rangarajan said an amount of 160 billion rupees indicated in the 1997/98 budget as "monetised fiscal deficit" representing government borrowings referred to RBI funding of primary issues of government securities.
Subsequently, the amount could be exceeded on account of open market borrowings by RBI depending on market conditions.
"I am happy this agreeement has been reached," Rangarajan said.
Ahluwalia said the new financing system would discipline fiscal spending but that did not mean a lack of flexibility. "Obviously there will be temporary mismatches," he said.

India is aiming to cut its fiscal deficit to 4.5 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997/98 from an expected 5.0 percent in 1996/97, and over the medium term cut the deficit to 3-4 percent.
